newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Bloodshed seals end of Algerian poll campaign.
newsitem.headline: Bloodshed seals end of Algerian poll campaign.

text.p: Bombs ripped through Algiers killing about 18 people and wounding more than 100 in less than 24 hours as campaigning closed for Algeria's parliamentary elections meant to end years of bloodshed.

One bomb exploded at 8.30 a.m. (0730 GMT) on Monday in the crowded Bouzrina market in the Moslem fundamentalist stronghold of Bab El-Oued in central Algiers. Security forces said it killed seven people and wounded 37.
"I heard a burst of gunfire and then the bomb exploded," a greengrocer in the market said.
State radio announced markets were being ordered to close from now until Friday, the day after polling takes place.
Less than three hours after the bomb blast, journalists in the city's Aurassi hotel -- in Algeria to cover Thursday's general election -- heard another powerful explosion.
This appeared to come from the western part of the city's downtown area. No details were immediately available.
On Sunday, two bombs ripped through buses in central Algiers. Officials said at least seven people died and 77 were wounded. Newspapers on Monday put the toll at 11 dead.

One Algiers resident said of Monday's bomb in Bab El-Oued: "Gunmen shot a woman schoolworker and then booby-trapped her bleeding body. Six people were gathered round her to try to help her when the bomb went off, killing all six."
Officials blame Moslem fundamentalists for hundreds of bombs and massacres over the past five years, during which Algeria's 29 million people have been without a parliament.

An estimated 60,000 people have died since January 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by the now-outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS). Thursday's ballot is seen by President Liamine Zeroual and his government as a way of ending the years of crisis.

But the bombing brought a cry of despair on Monday: "Even during the (independence) war against France we did not see such horrors," said one of several shocked women, wearing the Moslem veil, near the pools of blood and severed limbs.
Troops and security forces began casting their ballots on Monday, to be free to guard the 16.77 million eligible electorate voting at 37,586 polling stations on Thursday.

Meanwhile, about 8,000 candidates, running under the flag of 39 parties or as independents, made last pitches for support in the race for the 380-seat National Assembly. Campaigning ends on Monday night to give voters time to reflect.
The final day's campaigning focused in Algiers where eight main party leaders are competing for seats in the city of an estimated three to four million people.

Moderate Islamist-oriented Movement for a Peaceful Society (MPS) leader Mahfoud Nanhah gathers his supporters in the 20,000-seat indoor Harcha stadium to hammer home his "Peace is the solution" message.

Hawkish anti-Islamist Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) chief Said Saadi meets his supporters a few hours later in the same stadium to urge them to back anti-Islamist candidates with the aim of establishing a secular multiparty democracy.
The National Democratic Rally (RND), grouping Zeroual's backers and seen as a frontrunner, was putting on a concert at another stadium to lure young voters.
